results.title: Continuous integration
results.content:
/en/actions/get-started/continuous-integration Continuous integration Continuous integration:  # Continuous integration

You can create custom continuous integration (CI) workflows directly in your GitHub repository with GitHub Actions.

## About continuous integration

Continuous integration (CI) is a software practice that requires frequently committing code to a shared repository. Committing code more often detects errors sooner and reduces the amount of code a developer needs to debug when finding the source of an error. Frequent code updates also make it easier to merge changes from different members of a software development team. This is great for developers, who can spend more time writing code and less time debugging errors or resolving merge conflicts.

When you commit code to your repository, you can continuously build and test the code to make sure that the commit doesn't introduce errors. Your tests can include code linters (which check style formatting), security checks, code coverage, functional tests, and other custom checks.

Building and testing your code requires a server. You can build and test updates locally before pushing code to a repository, or you can use a CI server that checks for new code commits in a repository.

## About continuous integration using GitHub Actions

CI using GitHub Actions offers workflows that can build the code in your repository and run your tests. Workflows can run on GitHub-hosted virtual machines, or on machines that you host yourself. For more information, see [GitHub-hosted runners](/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/about-github-hosted-runners) and [Self-hosted runners](/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners/managing-self-hosted-runners/about-self-hosted-runners).

You can configure your CI workflow to run when a GitHub event occurs (for example, when new code is pushed to your repository), on a set schedule, or when an external event occurs using the repository dispatch webhook.

GitHub runs your CI tests and provides the results of each test in the pull request, so you can see whether the change in your branch introduces an error. When all CI tests in a workflow pass, the changes you pushed are ready to be reviewed by a team member or merged. When a test fails, one of your changes may have caused the failure.

When you set up CI in your repository, GitHub analyzes the code in your repository and recommends CI workflows based on the language and framework in your repository. For example, if you use [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/), GitHub will suggest a workflow template that installs your Node.js packages and runs your tests. You can use the CI workflow template suggested by GitHub, customize the suggested workflow template, or create your own custom workflow file to run your CI tests.

In addition to helping you set up CI workflows for your project, you can use GitHub Actions to create workflows across the full software development life cycle. For example, you can use actions to deploy, package, or release your project. For more information, see [Writing workflows](/en/actions/learn-github-actions).

For a definition of common terms, see [Understanding GitHub Actions](/en/actions/learn-github-actions/understanding-github-actions).

## Next steps

GitHub offers CI workflow templates for a variety of languages and frameworks. For tutorials on setting up continuous integration with these templates, see [Building and testing your code](/en/actions/use-cases-and-examples/building-and-testing).

results.title: Continuous deployment
results.content:
/en/actions/get-started/continuous-deployment Continuous deployment Continuous deployment:  # Continuous deployment

You can create custom continuous deployment (CD) workflows directly in your GitHub repository with GitHub Actions.

## About continuous deployment

*Continuous deployment* (CD) is the practice of using automation to publish and deploy software updates. As part of the typical CD process, the code is automatically built and tested before deployment.

Continuous deployment is often coupled with continuous integration. For more information about continuous integration, see [Continuous integration](/en/actions/automating-builds-and-tests/about-continuous-integration).

## About continuous deployment using GitHub Actions

You can set up a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy your software product. To verify that your product works as expected, your workflow can build the code in your repository and run your tests before deploying.

You can configure your CD workflow to run when an event occurs (for example, when new code is pushed to the default branch of your repository), on a set schedule, manually, or when an external event occurs using the repository dispatch webhook. For more information about when your workflow can run, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows).

GitHub Actions provides features that give you more control over deployments. For example, you can use environments to require approval for a job to proceed, restrict which branches can trigger a workflow, or limit access to secrets. You can use concurrency to limit your CD pipeline to a maximum of one in-progress deployment. For more information about these features, see [Deploying with GitHub Actions](/en/actions/deployment/about-deployments/deploying-with-github-actions) and [Managing environments for deployment](/en/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/managing-environments-for-deployment).

## Workflow templates and third-party actions

GitHub offers deployment workflow templates for several popular services, such as Azure Web App. To learn how to get started using a workflow template, see [Using workflow templates](/en/actions/learn-github-actions/using-starter-workflows) or [browse the full list of deployment workflow templates](https://github.com/actions/starter-workflows/tree/main/deployments). You can also check out our more detailed guides for specific deployment workflows, such as [Deploying Node.js to Azure App Service](/en/actions/deployment/deploying-to-your-cloud-provider/deploying-to-azure/deploying-nodejs-to-azure-app-service).

Many service providers also offer actions on GitHub Marketplace for deploying to their service. For the full list, see [GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?category=deployment\&type=actions).

## Next steps

If your GitHub Actions workflows need to access resources from a cloud provider that supports OpenID Connect (OIDC), you can configure your workflows to authenticate directly to the cloud provider. This will let you stop storing these credentials as long-lived secrets and provide other security benefits. For more information, see [OpenID Connect](/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect).

results.title: About GitHub Packages and GitHub Actions
results.content:
/en/packages/managing-github-packages-using-github-actions-workflows/about-github-packages-and-github-actions About GitHub Packages and GitHub Actions About GitHub Packages and GitHub Actions:  # About GitHub Packages and GitHub Actions

Learn the fundamentals of managing packages through your GitHub Actions workflows.

<!-- 2148AF7B-5FF8-4B28-A808-D692FEE2225A -->

## Packaging in continuous integration workflows

A packaging step is a common part of a continuous integration or continuous delivery workflow. Creating a package at the end of a continuous integration workflow can help during code reviews on a pull request.

After building and testing your code, a packaging step can produce a runnable or deployable artifact. Depending on the kind of application you're building, this package can be downloaded locally for manual testing, made available for users to download, or deployed to a staging or production environment.

For example, a continuous integration workflow for a Java project may run `mvn package` to produce a JAR file. Or, a CI workflow for a Node.js application may create a Docker container.

Now, when reviewing a pull request, you'll be able to look at the workflow run and download the artifact that was produced.

![Screenshot of the "Artifacts" section of a workflow run. The name of the artifact generated by the run, "artifact," is outlined in orange.](/assets/images/help/repository/artifact-drop-down-updated.png)
This will let you run the code in the pull request on your machine, which can help with debugging or testing the pull request.

## Workflows for publishing packages

In addition to uploading packaging artifacts for testing in a continuous integration workflow, you can create workflows that build your project and publish packages to a package registry.

* **Publish packages to GitHub Packages**
  GitHub Packages can act as a package hosting service for many types of packages. You can choose to share your packages with all of GitHub, or private packages to share with collaborators or an organization. For more information, see [Introduction to GitHub Packages](/en/packages/learn-github-packages/introduction-to-github-packages).

  You may want to publish packages to GitHub Packages on every push into the default branch. This will allow developers on your project to always be able to run and test the latest build from the default branch easily, by installing it from GitHub Packages.

* **Publish packages to a package registry:**
  For many projects, publishing to a package registry is performed whenever a new version of a project is released. For example, a project that produces a JAR file may upload new releases to the Maven Central repository. Or, a .NET project may produce a nuget package and upload it to the NuGet Gallery.

  You can automate this by creating a workflow that publishes packages to a package registry on every release creation. For more information, see [Managing releases in a repository](/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository).

I'll help you understand CI/CD pipeline setup with GitHub Actions. Let me load detailed guidance on this topic.I'd be happy to help you set up a CI/CD pipeline! To give you the best guidance, I need to understand your needs better:

1. **What's your project type?** (e.g., Node.js, Python, Java, Go, .NET, etc.)
2. **What do you want to automate?** (e.g., tests, linting, builds, deployments, security scans)
3. **Where are you deploying?** (e.g., AWS, Azure, Heroku, Docker registry, GitHub Pages, etc.)
4. **Do you have a specific GitHub repository?** (I can help set it up directly)

**In the meantime, here's a quick overview of setting up CI/CD with GitHub Actions:**

### Basic Steps:

1. **Create a workflow file** in `.github/workflows/` directory (e.g., `ci.yml`)
2. **Define triggers** (on push, pull request, schedule, etc.)
3. **Set up jobs** for testing, building, linting
4. **Add deployment steps** if needed
5. **Monitor results** in the PR checks section

### Quick Example (Node.js):
```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
```

**What would be most helpful to start with?**

references.instructions:
<overview>
    <purpose>
      A structured approach for agents to comprehensively explore all entities associated
      with a GitHub Pull Request. This ability provides the entity model, traversal strategy,
      and prioritization logic so the agent fetches the right scoped data in the right priority order.
    </purpose>
</overview>

<entity_model>
    <description>
      A PR connects to entities across five domains. Think of these as concentric rings
      radiating out from the PR core. Each successive ring is more expensive to fetch
      and less universally relevant.
    </description>
    <ring id="0" name="PR Core" fetch_policy="always_fetch_first">
      <description>
        These fields are available on the PR object itself and cost one API call.
      </description>
      <entity_group name="metadata">
        <field>number</field>
        <field>title</field>
        <field>body (description)</field>
        <field>state (open/closed/merged)</field>
        <field>draft status</field>
      </entity_group>
      <entity name="files_changed" priority="1">
        <reveals>Scope of change — file count, additions, deletions</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>Almost always — gives you the "shape" of the PR. These aggregate counts (file count, additions, deletions) live on the PR object itself, so they cost no extra call. Fetching the per-file list or diffs is a separate Ring 2 step (individual_file_diffs).</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="1" name="First-degree entities" fetch_policy="fetch_based_on_intent">
      <description>
        Each requires one additional call per entity type. Fetch based on user intent.
      </description>
      <entity name="commits" priority="5">
        <reveals>Granularity of changes, commit messages, co-authors</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When investigating what changed or commit hygiene</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="reviews" priority="1">
        <reveals>Approval state, who reviewed, blocking reviews</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When assessing merge readiness or understanding decisions</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="review_comments" priority="4">
        <reveals>Line-level feedback, unresolved threads</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding specific technical discussions</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="issue_comments" priority="6">
        <reveals>Conversation on the PR itself (non-inline)</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When tracing decisions or understanding context</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="check_runs" priority="2">
        <reveals>CI status, which checks passed/failed/pending</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When debugging failures or assessing merge readiness</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="2" name="Second-degree entities" fetch_policy="fetch_selectively">
      <description>
        These require following references from Ring 1 entities. Only fetch after
        Ring 1 data is in hand.
      </description>
      <entity name="linked_closing_issues">
        <reached_via>PR body ("Closes #N") or timeline events</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding the why behind a PR</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="individual_file_diffs">
        <reached_via>Files changed list</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When the user asks about specific code changes</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="check_run_annotations">
        <reached_via>Failed check runs</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When debugging a specific CI failure</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="deployment_statuses">
        <reached_via>Check suites or deployments API</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When investigating deploy/preview state</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="commit_statuses_legacy">
        <reached_via>Individual commits</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When checks API returns incomplete info</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="review_thread_resolution">
        <reached_via>Review comments</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When tracking unresolved feedback</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="3" name="Contextual entities" fetch_policy="fetch_only_when_needed">
      <description>
        These provide broader context but are expensive or tangential. Only fetch
        when Ring 0-2 data doesn't fully answer the question or user explicitly asks.
      </description>
      <entity name="referenced_issues_and_prs">
        <reached_via>Issue and PR links in the PR description</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When need even deeper understanding of the intent of a PR</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="documentation_links">
        <reached_via>Documentation links in the PR description</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>
          When need the deepest understanding for the approaches taken in the PR.
          Be cautious — these can lead you down a rabbit hole so ask the user if they want to follow them before fetching.
        </when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="project_board_status">
        <when_to_fetch>When tracking workflow state</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="timeline_events">
        <when_to_fetch>When building a chronological narrative</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="branch_protection_rules">
        <when_to_fetch>When diagnosing why a PR can't merge</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="codeowners">
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding required reviewers</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="repository_rulesets">
        <when_to_fetch>When diagnosing merge policy enforcement</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      
    </ring>
</entity_model> 

<traversal_strategy>
    <step order="0" name="determine_user_intent">
      <instruction>
        Before fetching anything beyond Ring 0, classify the user's question into
        one or more of these intents.
      </instruction>
      <intent id="status_check">
        <description>What's the state of this PR?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (reviews, checks)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="merge_readiness">
        <description>Is this ready to merge? Why can't this merge?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (reviews, checks, files), 2 (branch protection, unresolved threads)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="debug_ci">
        <description>Why is CI failing?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (checks), 2 (annotations, logs)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="review_summary">
        <description>What feedback was given?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (reviews, review comments, issue comments)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="change_understanding">
        <description>What does this PR do?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (files, commits), 2 (linked issues, diffs)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="decision_trace">
        <description>Why was this approach chosen?</description>
        <rings>0, 1 (all comments), 2 (linked issues), 3 (timeline, referenced issues and prs)</rings>
      </intent>
      <intent id="full_investigation">
        <description>Tell me everything about this PR.</description>
        <rings>All rings, prioritized</rings>
      </intent>
    </step>
 
    <step order="1" name="fetch_ring_0_and_assess">
      <instruction>
        Always start by fetching the PR core. From Ring 0 alone, you can often:
      </instruction>
      <capabilities>
        <capability>Answer simple status questions immediately</capability>
        <capability>Determine if the PR is merged/closed (which changes what's relevant)</capability>
        <capability>Read the description for linked issue references to guide Ring 2 fetching</capability>
        <capability>Check labels for context (e.g., "bug", "breaking-change", "do-not-merge")</capability>
      </capabilities>
      <guideline name="use_preloaded_data">
        If the conversation context or page context already contains Ring 0 PR data
        (title, body, state, draft status, author, labels, assignees, milestone, and
        the change shape: file count, additions, deletions), do NOT re-fetch it via a
        GET /pulls/{number} tool call. Ring 1 entities (reviews, check runs, the
        per-file list, commits, review comments, issue comments) are NOT preloaded and
        still require tool calls when the user's intent demands them.
      </guideline>
    </step>
 
    <step order="2" name="fan_out_to_ring_1">
      <instruction>
        Based on the intent classification, fetch Ring 1 entities in parallel where
        possible. If you must serialize, use this priority order (highest signal-to-token
        ratio first):
      </instruction>
      <priority_order>
        <item priority="1">Reviews — highest signal-to-token ratio for most intents</item>
        <item priority="2">Check runs — critical for status/merge/debug intents</item>
        <item priority="3">Files changed (stat only, not full diff) — shapes understanding of scope</item>
        <item priority="4">Review comments — detailed but potentially voluminous</item>
        <item priority="5">Commits — useful but often redundant with files changed</item>

    <purpose>
      A structured approach for agents to comprehensively explore all entities associated
      with a GitHub Pull Request. This ability provides the entity model, traversal strategy,
      and prioritization logic so the agent fetches the right scoped data in the right priority order.
    </purpose>

    <description>

      radiating out from the PR core. Each successive ring is more expensive to fetch
      and less universally relevant.

      <description>

      </description>

        <field>number</field>
        <field>title</field>
        <field>body (description)</field>
        <field>state (open/closed/merged)</field>
        <field>draft status</field>

      <entity name="files_changed" priority="1">
        <reveals>Scope of change — file count, additions, deletions</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>Almost always — gives you the "shape" of the PR. These aggregate counts (file count, additions, deletions) live on the PR object itself, so they cost no extra call. Fetching the per-file list or diffs is a separate Ring 2 step (individual_file_diffs).</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="1" name="First-degree entities" fetch_policy="fetch_based_on_intent">
      <description>
        Each requires one additional call per entity type. Fetch based on user intent.
      </description>
      <entity name="commits" priority="5">
        <reveals>Granularity of changes, commit messages, co-authors</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When investigating what changed or commit hygiene</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="reviews" priority="1">
        <reveals>Approval state, who reviewed, blocking reviews</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When assessing merge readiness or understanding decisions</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="review_comments" priority="4">
        <reveals>Line-level feedback, unresolved threads</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding specific technical discussions</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="issue_comments" priority="6">
        <reveals>Conversation on the PR itself (non-inline)</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When tracing decisions or understanding context</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
      <entity name="check_runs" priority="2">
        <reveals>CI status, which checks passed/failed/pending</reveals>
        <when_to_fetch>When debugging failures or assessing merge readiness</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>
    <ring id="2" name="Second-degree entities" fetch_policy="fetch_selectively">
      <description>
        These require following references from Ring 1 entities. Only fetch after
        Ring 1 data is in hand.
      </description>

        <reached_via>PR body ("Closes #N") or timeline events</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When understanding the why behind a PR</when_to_fetch>

        <when_to_fetch>When the user asks about specific code changes</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>

      </entity>
      <entity name="review_thread_resolution">
        <reached_via>Review comments</reached_via>
        <when_to_fetch>When tracking unresolved feedback</when_to_fetch>
      </entity>
    </ring>

results.title: Continuous integration
results.content:
/en/actions/get-started/continuous-integration Continuous integration Continuous integration:  # Continuous integration

You can create custom continuous integration (CI) workflows directly in your GitHub repository with GitHub Actions.

## About continuous integration

Continuous integration (CI) is a software practice that requires frequently committing code to a shared repository. Committing code more often detects errors sooner and reduces the amount of code a developer needs to debug when finding the source of an error. Frequent code updates also make it easier to merge changes from different members of a software development team. This is great for developers, who can spend more time writing code and less time debugging errors or resolving merge conflicts.

When you commit code to your repository, you can continuously build and test the code to make sure that the commit doesn't introduce errors. Your tests can include code linters (which check style formatting), security checks, code coverage, functional tests, and other custom checks.

Building and testing your code requires a server. You can build and test updates locally before pushing code to a repository, or you can use a CI server that checks for new code commits in a repository.

## About continuous integration using GitHub Actions

CI using GitHub Actions offers workflows that can build the code in your repository and run your tests. Workflows can run on GitHub-hosted virtual machines, or on machines that you host yourself. For more information, see [GitHub-hosted runners](/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/about-github-hosted-runners) and [Self-hosted runners](/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners/managing-self-hosted-runners/about-self-hosted-runners).

You can configure your CI workflow to run when a GitHub event occurs (for example, when new code is pushed to your repository), on a set schedule, or when an external event occurs using the repository dispatch webhook.

GitHub runs your CI tests and provides the results of each test in the pull request, so you can see whether the change in your branch introduces an error. When all CI tests in a workflow pass, the changes you pushed are ready to be reviewed by a team member or merged. When a test fails, one of your changes may have caused the failure.

When you set up CI in your repository, GitHub analyzes the code in your repository and recommends CI workflows based on the language and framework in your repository. For example, if you use [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/), GitHub will suggest a workflow template that installs your Node.js packages and runs your tests. You can use the CI workflow template suggested by GitHub, customize the suggested workflow template, or create your own custom workflow file to run your CI tests.

In addition to helping you set up CI workflows for your project, you can use GitHub Actions to create workflows across the full software development life cycle. For example, you can use actions to deploy, package, or release your project. For more information, see [Writing workflows](/en/actions/learn-github-actions).

For a definition of common terms, see [Understanding GitHub Actions](/en/actions/learn-github-actions/understanding-github-actions).

## Next steps

GitHub offers CI workflow templates for a variety of languages and frameworks. For tutorials on setting up continuous integration with these templates, see [Building and testing your code](/en/actions/use-cases-and-examples/building-and-testing).

results.title: Publishing and installing a package with GitHub Actions
results.content:
/en/packages/managing-github-packages-using-github-actions-workflows/publishing-and-installing-a-package-with-github-actions Publishing and installing a package with GitHub Actions Publishing and installing a package with GitHub Actions:  #
jobs:
  # This pushes the image to GitHub Packages.
  push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write
      contents: read
      #
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build . --file Dockerfile --tag $IMAGE_NAME --label "runnumber=${GITHUB_RUN_ID}"

      - name: Log in to registry
        run: echo "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        #
      - name: Push image
        run: |
          IMAGE_ID=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/$IMAGE_NAME

          # This changes all uppercase characters to lowercase.
          IMAGE_ID=$(echo $IMAGE_ID | tr '[A-Z]' '[a-z]')
          # This strips the git ref prefix from the version.
          VERSION=$(echo "${{ github.ref }}" | sed -e 's,.*/\(.*\),\1,')
          # This strips the "v" prefix from the tag name.
          [[ "${{ github.ref }}" == "refs/tags/"* ]] && VERSION=$(echo $VERSION | sed -e 's/^v//')
          # This uses the Docker `latest` tag convention.
          [ "$VERSION" == "main" ] && VERSION=latest
          echo IMAGE_ID=$IMAGE_ID
          echo VERSION=$VERSION
          docker tag $IMAGE_NAME $IMAGE_ID:$VERSION
          docker push $IMAGE_ID:$VERSION
```

results.title: Continuous deployment
results.content:
/en/actions/get-started/continuous-deployment Continuous deployment Continuous deployment:  # Continuous deployment

You can create custom continuous deployment (CD) workflows directly in your GitHub repository with GitHub Actions.

## About continuous deployment

*Continuous deployment* (CD) is the practice of using automation to publish and deploy software updates. As part of the typical CD process, the code is automatically built and tested before deployment.

Continuous deployment is often coupled with continuous integration. For more information about continuous integration, see [Continuous integration](/en/actions/automating-builds-and-tests/about-continuous-integration).

## About continuous deployment using GitHub Actions

You can set up a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy your software product. To verify that your product works as expected, your workflow can build the code in your repository and run your tests before deploying.

You can configure your CD workflow to run when an event occurs (for example, when new code is pushed to the default branch of your repository), on a set schedule, manually, or when an external event occurs using the repository dispatch webhook. For more information about when your workflow can run, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows).

GitHub Actions provides features that give you more control over deployments. For example, you can use environments to require approval for a job to proceed, restrict which branches can trigger a workflow, or limit access to secrets. You can use concurrency to limit your CD pipeline to a maximum of one in-progress deployment. For more information about these features, see [Deploying with GitHub Actions](/en/actions/deployment/about-deployments/deploying-with-github-actions) and [Managing environments for deployment](/en/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/managing-environments-for-deployment).

## Workflow templates and third-party actions

GitHub offers deployment workflow templates for several popular services, such as Azure Web App. To learn how to get started using a workflow template, see [Using workflow templates](/en/actions/learn-github-actions/using-starter-workflows) or [browse the full list of deployment workflow templates](https://github.com/actions/starter-workflows/tree/main/deployments). You can also check out our more detailed guides for specific deployment workflows, such as [Deploying Node.js to Azure App Service](/en/actions/deployment/deploying-to-your-cloud-provider/deploying-to-azure/deploying-nodejs-to-azure-app-service).

Many service providers also offer actions on GitHub Marketplace for deploying to their service. For the full list, see [GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?category=deployment\&type=actions).

## Next steps

If your GitHub Actions workflows need to access resources from a cloud provider that supports OpenID Connect (OIDC), you can configure your workflows to authenticate directly to the cloud provider. This will let you stop storing these credentials as long-lived secrets and provide other security benefits. For more information, see [OpenID Connect](/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect).

You can configure your CI workflow to run when a GitHub event occurs (for example, when new code is pushed to your repository), on a set schedule, or when an external event occurs using the repository dispatch webhook.

GitHub runs your CI tests and provides the results of each test in the pull request, so you can see whether the change in your branch introduces an error. When all CI tests in a workflow pass, the changes you pushed are ready to be reviewed by a team member or merged. When a test fails, one of your changes may have caused the failure.

When you set up CI in your repository, GitHub analyzes the code in your repository and recommends CI workflows based on the language and framework in your repository. For example, if you use [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/), GitHub will suggest a workflow template that installs your Node.js packages and runs your tests. You can use the CI workflow template suggested by GitHub, customize the suggested workflow template, or create your own custom workflow file to run your CI tests.

In addition to helping you set up CI workflows for your project, you can use GitHub Actions to create workflows across the full software development life cycle. For example, you can use actions to deploy, package, or release your project. For more information, see [Writing workflows](/en/actions/learn-github-actions).

For a definition of common terms, see [Understanding GitHub Actions](/en/actions/learn-github-actions/understanding-github-actions).

## Next steps

GitHub offers CI workflow templates for a variety of languages and frameworks. For tutorials on setting up continuous integration with these templates, see [Building and testing your code](/en/actions/use-cases-and-examples/building-and-testing).

results.title: Publishing and installing a package with GitHub Actions
results.content:
/en/packages/managing-github-packages-using-github-actions-workflows/publishing-and-installing-a-package-with-github-actions Publishing and installing a package with GitHub Actions Publishing and installing a package with GitHub Actions:  #
jobs:
  # This pushes the image to GitHub Packages.
  push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write
      contents: read
      #
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Build image
        run: docker build . --file Dockerfile --tag $IMAGE_NAME --label "runnumber=${GITHUB_RUN_ID}"

      - name: Log in to registry
        run: echo "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        #
      - name: Push image
        run: |
          IMAGE_ID=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/$IMAGE_NAME

          # This changes all uppercase characters to lowercase.
          IMAGE_ID=$(echo $IMAGE_ID | tr '[A-Z]' '[a-z]')
          # This strips the git ref prefix from the version.
          VERSION=$(echo "${{ github.ref }}" | sed -e 's,.*/\(.*\),\1,')
          # This strips the "v" prefix from the tag name.
          [[ "${{ github.ref }}" == "refs/tags/"* ]] && VERSION=$(echo $VERSION | sed -e 's/^v//')
          # This uses the Docker `latest` tag convention.
          [ "$VERSION" == "main" ] && VERSION=latest
          echo IMAGE_ID=$IMAGE_ID
          echo VERSION=$VERSION
          docker tag $IMAGE_NAME $IMAGE_ID:$VERSION
          docker push $IMAGE_ID:$VERSION
```

results.title: Continuous deployment
results.content:
/en/actions/get-started/continuous-deployment Continuous deployment Continuous deployment:  # Continuous deployment

You can create custom continuous deployment (CD) workflows directly in your GitHub repository with GitHub Actions.

## About continuous deployment

*Continuous deployment* (CD) is the practice of using automation to publish and deploy software updates. As part of the typical CD process, the code is automatically built and tested before deployment.

Continuous deployment is often coupled with continuous integration. For more information about continuous integration, see [Continuous integration](/en/actions/automating-builds-and-tests/about-continuous-integration).

## About continuous deployment using GitHub Actions

You can set up a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy your software product. To verify that your product works as expected, your workflow can build the code in your repository and run your tests before deploying.

You can configure your CD workflow to run when an event occurs (for example, when new code is pushed to the default branch of your repository), on a set schedule, manually, or when an external event occurs using the repository dispatch webhook. For more information about when your workflow can run, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows).

GitHub Actions provides features that give you more control over deployments. For example, you can use environments to require approval for a job to proceed, restrict which branches can trigger a workflow, or limit access to secrets. You can use concurrency to limit your CD pipeline to a maximum of one in-progress deployment. For more information about these features, see [Deploying with GitHub Actions](/en/actions/deployment/about-deployments/deploying-with-github-actions) and [Managing environments for deployment](/en/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/managing-environments-for-deployment).

## Workflow templates and third-party actions

GitHub offers deployment workflow templates for several popular services, such as Azure Web App. To learn how to get started using a workflow template, see [Using workflow templates](/en/actions/learn-github-actions/using-starter-workflows) or [browse the full list of deployment workflow templates](https://github.com/actions/starter-workflows/tree/main/deployments). You can also check out our more detailed guides for specific deployment workflows, such as [Deploying Node.js to Azure App Service](/en/actions/deployment/deploying-to-your-cloud-provider/deploying-to-azure/deploying-nodejs-to-azure-app-service).

Many service providers also offer actions on GitHub Marketplace for deploying to their service. For the full list, see [GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?category=deployment\&type=actions).

## Next steps

If your GitHub Actions workflows need to access resources from a cloud provider that supports OpenID Connect (OIDC), you can configure your workflows to authenticate directly to the cloud provider. This will let you stop storing these credentials as long-lived secrets and provide other security benefits. For more information, see [OpenID Connect](/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect).
